extracted.intended_audience: researchers, university press officers, science communicators, and health journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for writing and evaluating academic press releases about health-related research, focused on avoiding forms of exaggeration that propagate into news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that go beyond what the underlying study supports (giving advice that outstrips the evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found 40% of press releases contained exaggerated advice; when press releases contained such exaggeration, 58% of news stories showed similar exaggeration. Avoid offering prescriptive or actionable recommendations unless they are clearly supported by the study's design, results, and context. Include qualifiers where appropriate and avoid overstating clinical or behavioral implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning correlation or association into statements of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 33% of press releases in the sample contained exaggerated causal claims; 81% of corresponding news stories also contained similar causal exaggeration. Do not describe associative findings as causal; explicitly state when findings are observational or correlational. Reserve causal language for studies with appropriate design/analysis (e.g., randomized controlled trials or robust causal inference methods), and explain limitations to causal interpretation when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated inference to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrapolating results from animal or cell studies to humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 36% of press releases extrapolated animal or cell research to humans; 86% of news stories mirrored this exaggeration. Avoid asserting human effects based on preclinical (animal or in vitro) studies. Clearly state the study organism/model and the limits of generalizability to humans; include warnings about the need for further research before human-relevant claims are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include caveats and limitations from the original study
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the study's caveats and limitations rather than omitting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend including caveats and limitations from the original paper in press releases to reduce misleading downstream coverage. Examples: sample size limitations, potential confounders, short follow-up, measurement limitations, and generalizability constraints. Explicitly summarise key limitations so journalists and readers understand the evidence strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match claims to actual study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure claims in the press release reflect the study's design and strength of evidence (e.g., RCT vs observational).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implicit rubric urges matching claims to study design: identify whether a study is a randomized controlled trial, observational study, animal research, in vitro work, etc., and tailor claim strength accordingly. Misstating study type or overstating implications relative to design contributes to downstream exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise accuracy over hype (improving press release accuracy to reduce misleading news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve accuracy of academic press releases as a practical way to reduce misleading health-related news; do not rely on hype to increase media uptake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found little evidence that exaggeration in press releases increased news uptake (i.e., hype did not significantly increase pickup rates). Therefore, press officers should prioritise accurate, cautious framing rather than sensational claims. When press releases avoid exaggeration, downstream news exaggeration is much lower.
